short: The price of borrowing money, shown as a percentage of the amount borrowed that the borrower pays the lender each year.
kid: When you borrow your friend's crayons, you give them back with one extra crayon to say thank you. The bigger the thank-you, the more it costs to borrow.
detail: An interest rate is the price of money over time: the percentage of a loan's principal that a borrower pays a lender each year, or that a saver earns on a deposit. Rates differ by borrower and by length of loan because they bundle several things: expected inflation, the lender's reward for waiting, compensation for the risk of not being repaid and, for longer loans, extra pay for locking money up. A central bank sets the anchor for short-term rates; in India, the RBI's repo rate feeds through to deposit, loan and bond rates. Rates matter across finance because they set companies' borrowing costs, the discount rate in valuations and the price of bonds, which fall when rates rise. A common confusion is between the quoted annual rate and the effective rate after compounding, which is higher when interest is added more than once a year.
example: Say you deposit ₹1,00,000 at 7% a year with interest paid once a year: you earn ₹7,000. If the bank instead compounds quarterly at 1.75% a quarter, you end the year with about ₹1,07,186, an effective annual rate of about 7.19%.
formula: Simple interest = Principal × Rate × Time; with compounding, Amount = Principal × (1 + r/n)^(n × t)

short: The interest rate as quoted on a loan, deposit or bond, before any adjustment for inflation.
kid: Your friend promises to give you back 10 sweets later. The number 10 is the promise you hear, even if sweets get smaller by then.
detail: The nominal interest rate is the stated rate in money terms: the 7% printed on a fixed deposit receipt, the coupon on a bond or the repo rate the RBI announces. It tells you how many more rupees you will have, not how much more you can buy with them. Because it includes expected inflation, nominal rates tend to be high in high-inflation economies and low where prices are stable, which is why comparing India's rates with Japan's tells you little without adjusting. Investors care about the real return, so they subtract inflation from the nominal rate. In bond markets, 'nominal yields' also distinguish ordinary government bonds from inflation-indexed ones, and some textbooks use 'nominal yield' to mean a bond's coupon rate. Do not confuse it with the 'nominal' annual rate quoted before compounding; context tells you which sense is meant.
example: Say a fixed deposit pays a nominal 7% a year and inflation runs at 5%. ₹1,00,000 grows to ₹1,07,000, but goods that cost ₹1,00,000 a year ago now cost ₹1,05,000, so your buying power rises by only about 1.9% (1,07,000 / 1,05,000 − 1).
formula: (1 + Nominal rate) = (1 + Real rate) × (1 + Expected inflation); approximately, Nominal rate ≈ Real rate + Expected inflation

short: The interest rate after removing inflation, which shows how much your buying power actually grows.
kid: Your piggy bank grows by a few coins, but sweets got pricier too. What matters is how many more sweets you can really buy.
detail: The real interest rate is, roughly, the nominal rate minus inflation, so it measures the true gain in buying power for a lender or the true cost for a borrower. An ex-ante real rate uses expected inflation; an ex-post rate uses the inflation that actually happened. Real rates drive economic decisions: when they are high, saving is rewarded and borrowing to invest or spend is discouraged, which is how central banks cool an economy. Negative real rates, when inflation exceeds the nominal rate, quietly erode savers' wealth. The RBI and other central banks watch the real policy rate, the policy rate minus expected inflation, to judge how tight policy is. Markets read real yields directly from inflation-indexed bonds such as US TIPS. A common mistake is treating a high nominal rate as attractive when inflation is just as high.
example: Say a government bond yields 7% and inflation is expected to be 4%. The approximate real rate is 3% (7 − 4); the exact figure is 1.07 / 1.04 − 1, or about 2.88%.
formula: Real rate ≈ Nominal rate − Inflation; exactly, Real rate = (1 + Nominal rate) / (1 + Inflation) − 1

short: The link between interest rates and inflation: the quoted interest rate roughly equals the real rate plus expected inflation.
kid: You lend a friend your toy and want one sweet back as thanks. If sweets are shrinking, you ask for a little extra sweet to make up for it.
detail: Named after the economist Irving Fisher, the Fisher equation says that lenders demand a nominal rate that covers both the real return they want and the inflation they expect. Written exactly, (1 + nominal) = (1 + real) × (1 + expected inflation); when rates are low, the shortcut nominal ≈ real + inflation works well. The Fisher effect is the idea that, over the long run, a rise in expected inflation pushes nominal rates up one for one, leaving real rates unchanged. The equation is used to back out inflation expectations from bond yields, to convert between nominal and real discount rates in valuation, and to explain why high-inflation countries have high interest rates. The common mistake is mixing the two: discount real cash flows at a real rate and nominal cash flows at a nominal rate, never one with the other.
example: If investors want a 2% real return and expect 5% inflation, the exact Fisher equation gives a nominal rate of 1.02 × 1.05 − 1 = 7.1%, while the shortcut gives 7%. The 0.1 percentage point gap is the cross term, 2% × 5%.
formula: (1 + i) = (1 + r) × (1 + π); approximately i ≈ r + π, where i is the nominal rate, r the real rate and π expected inflation

short: One hundredth of one percentage point, or 0.01%. It is used to describe small changes in interest rates precisely.
kid: Cut a big cake into a hundred slices, then cut one slice into a hundred crumbs. A basis point is like one crumb: a tiny unit for talking about tiny changes.
detail: A basis point (bp, plural bps, sometimes said 'bips') is 0.01 percentage point, so 100 basis points equal one percentage point. Markets use it because percentages invite confusion: if a 6% rate rises by '1%', it is unclear whether it went to 7% or 6.06%. Saying 100 bps or 6 bps removes the doubt. Central banks typically move policy rates in steps of 25 bps, and the RBI's repo-rate changes are reported this way, as are moves in bond yields, credit spreads, loan pricing and fund expense ratios. Because one basis point is tiny, it matters most on large sums: on a ₹10,000 crore loan book, 1 bp is ₹1 crore a year. The common confusion is equating a basis point with 1%; it is one hundredth of a percentage point.
example: Say a central bank raises its policy rate from 6.00% to 6.25%: that is a 25 bp hike. If a home loan rate rises by the same 25 bps, a ₹50 lakh balance costs an extra ₹12,500 a year in interest (0.25% × ₹50 lakh).
formula: 1 basis point = 0.01% = 0.0001; 100 basis points = 1 percentage point

short: The simple difference between two percentages. A rate moving from 4% to 6% has risen 2 percentage points, which is a 50% increase.
kid: If 4 of your 100 marbles were red and now 6 are red, you have 2 more red marbles. Counting the extra ones is the simplest way to say what changed.
detail: A percentage point (pp or ppt) measures the plain arithmetic difference between two percentages. If inflation falls from 6% to 4%, it has fallen by 2 percentage points, but by 33% in relative terms, because 2 is one third of 6. Mixing the two is one of the most common errors in financial writing, and it can make a change look much bigger or smaller than it really is. Economists and journalists use percentage points for changes in interest rates, margins, market shares and unemployment. In interest-rate markets the finer unit is the basis point: one percentage point equals 100 basis points. When you read that a rate 'rose 10%', check whether the writer means 10 percentage points or a 10% relative increase, because the two are very different.
example: Say ABC Ltd's operating margin improves from 12% to 15%. That is a rise of 3 percentage points, or a 25% relative increase (3 / 12). In basis points, it is 300 bps.
formula: Change in percentage points = New percentage − Old percentage; Relative change (%) = (New − Old) / Old × 100

short: A chart plotting the interest rates on government bonds against how long they have left to run, from a few months to decades.
kid: If you lend your toy for a day, you might ask for one sweet; for a whole month, maybe more. Draw a line of how many sweets you ask for each wait, and that line is the curve.
detail: The yield curve plots the yields of bonds with the same credit quality, usually government securities, against their time to maturity. It is also called the term structure of interest rates. Its shape summarises what markets expect: a normal curve slopes upward because investors want more for lending longer; an inverted curve, with short yields above long ones, has preceded many US recessions; flat and humped curves sit in between. The short end tracks the central bank's policy rate, while the long end reflects expected growth, inflation and a term premium. Banks, which borrow short and lend long, earn more when the curve is steep. In India, the curve is built from government securities, with the 10-year G-sec as the benchmark. Do not confuse the curve's level, how high rates are, with its slope, the gap between long and short yields.
example: Suppose 3-month, 2-year, 10-year and 30-year government bonds yield 4.0%, 4.3%, 4.8% and 5.1%. Plotted against maturity, the points rise from left to right, giving a normal, upward-sloping curve with a 2-year to 10-year spread of 50 basis points.

short: A yield curve that slopes upward, meaning longer-term bonds pay higher interest than shorter-term ones. It is the most common shape.
kid: If you let a friend keep your toy for longer, you ask for more sweets in return. Longer wait, bigger thank-you: that is the usual way.
detail: A normal yield curve slopes upward: yields rise as maturity lengthens, so a 10-year bond pays more than a 2-year bond, which pays more than a 3-month bill. It is called normal because it is the shape seen most of the time. Two forces explain it: investors demand a term premium for tying up money longer and bearing more price risk, and markets often expect short-term rates to stay steady or rise as the economy grows. A normal curve usually signals healthy growth expectations and helps banks, which fund long-term loans with short-term deposits. A very steep upward curve often appears early in a recovery, after a central bank has cut rates. Do not read 'normal' as 'good' in every case: a curve can slope upward because markets fear rising inflation or heavy government borrowing.
example: Suppose the 1-year government bond yields 5.5% and the 10-year yields 6.5%. The curve slopes upward with a 1-year to 10-year spread of 100 basis points, so an investor earns an extra 1 percentage point a year for lending for 10 years instead of 1.

short: A yield curve where short-term bonds pay more than long-term ones, a rare shape often read as a warning of recession.
kid: Usually you ask for more sweets when you lend your toy for longer. When friends offer fewer sweets for a long wait than a short one, something feels odd, and grown-ups start to worry.
detail: An inverted yield curve slopes downward: short-term yields sit above long-term ones, so a 2-year bond or a 3-month bill pays more than a 10-year bond. It usually appears when a central bank has pushed short rates up to fight inflation while investors expect slower growth and future rate cuts, which holds long yields down. In the US, inversions of the 3-month/10-year spread have preceded every recession since the late 1960s, with lags of roughly 6 to 24 months, but there have been false alarms too: the long 2022-24 inversion was not followed by a recession in 2023 or 2024. Inversion squeezes bank margins and can tighten lending. Treat it as a warning light, not a timer; the curve often turns positive again shortly before a downturn begins.
example: After a brief dip in spring 2022, the US 2-year Treasury yield moved lastingly above the 10-year in July 2022, and the curve stayed inverted until around September 2024, one of the longest stretches on record. Say the 2-year yields 4.8% and the 10-year 4.2%: the 2s10s spread is 4.2 − 4.8 = −0.6 percentage point, or −60 basis points.

short: A yield curve where short-term and long-term bonds pay about the same interest, often seen when the economy is changing direction.
kid: Your friend offers the same number of sweets whether you lend your toy for a day or a whole year. Waiting longer gets you nothing extra.
detail: A flat yield curve shows little difference between short- and long-term yields, for example a 2-year bond and a 10-year bond both yielding close to 6%. It often appears during transitions: when a central bank is raising rates late in an expansion, short yields climb toward long yields; when the economy slows, the curve can pass through flat on its way to inverting or back to normal. Because investors earn almost nothing extra for lending longer, many prefer short-dated bonds, which carry less price risk. Banks find it harder to profit from borrowing short and lending long, so lending can slow. A flat curve is not a forecast by itself; what matters is how it got there and where it is heading, so analysts read it alongside spreads and policy expectations.
example: Suppose the 2-year government bond yields 6.10% and the 10-year yields 6.20%. The 2-year to 10-year spread is only 10 basis points, so an investor gains just 0.10 percentage point a year for committing money for 8 extra years.

short: A yield curve where medium-term bonds pay more than both short-term and long-term bonds, so the line rises and then falls.
kid: Your friend offers more sweets for lending your toy for a month than for a day. But for a whole year, the offer drops again, like a little hill.
detail: A humped, or bell-shaped, yield curve rises from the short end to a peak at intermediate maturities, often 2 to 5 years, and then declines toward the long end. It is uncommon and usually short-lived. It can arise when markets expect rates to rise in the near term, as a central bank tightens, and then to fall later as growth slows. Supply and demand also matter: heavy buying of long bonds by pension funds and insurers can push long yields below medium-term ones. Some analysts treat a hump as an early sign that the curve may flatten or invert. The common mistake is calling any curve with small wiggles humped; the term applies when the middle clearly sits above both ends.
example: Suppose 1-year, 5-year and 30-year government bonds yield 5.0%, 5.6% and 5.2%. The 5-year sits 60 basis points above the 1-year and 40 basis points above the 30-year, so the curve rises and then falls, forming a hump.

short: A widening gap between long-term and short-term bond yields, so the yield curve slopes more steeply upward.
kid: Before, your friend gave one extra sweet for a long wait. Now they give three extra. The reward for waiting has grown bigger.
detail: Steepening means the spread between long and short yields, often measured as the 10-year minus the 2-year, is widening. Traders split it by cause. A bull steepener happens when short yields fall faster than long yields, typically because markets expect central bank rate cuts; it is common at the start of an easing cycle. A bear steepener happens when long yields rise faster than short ones, often on fears of higher inflation, heavy government borrowing or a rising term premium. A steepener is also a trade that profits from this widening, usually buying short-dated bonds and selling long-dated ones in duration-matched amounts. Steeper curves generally help bank margins. The confusion to avoid: 'bull' and 'bear' refer to bond prices, not shares, so a bull steepener means falling yields.
example: Say the 2-year yield falls from 4.50% to 4.00% while the 10-year yield falls from 4.30% to 4.20%. The 2s10s spread moves from −20 to +20 basis points, a 40 bp bull steepening.
formula: Change in slope = Change in (Long-term yield − Short-term yield); a positive change is steepening

short: A narrowing gap between long-term and short-term bond yields, so the yield curve becomes flatter.
kid: Before, your friend gave three extra sweets for a long wait. Now they give only one extra. Waiting longer is worth less than it was.
detail: Flattening means the spread between long and short yields is shrinking. A bear flattener happens when short yields rise faster than long ones, the classic pattern when a central bank is raising rates to fight inflation. A bull flattener happens when long yields fall faster than short ones, often because investors expect slower growth or lower inflation and move into long bonds. Persistent flattening can end in an inverted curve, which is why markets watch it as a late-cycle signal. A flattener is also a trade that profits from the narrowing, typically selling short-dated bonds and buying long-dated ones in duration-matched amounts. Flatter curves squeeze bank margins. Remember that 'bull' and 'bear' refer to bond prices: in a bull flattener, yields fall and bond prices rise.
example: Say the 2-year yield rises from 3.00% to 3.75% while the 10-year rises from 4.00% to 4.25%. The 2s10s spread narrows from 100 to 50 basis points, a 50 bp bear flattening.
formula: Change in slope = Change in (Long-term yield − Short-term yield); a negative change is flattening

short: The gap between a long-term and a short-term government bond yield, such as 10-year minus 2-year. It shows how steep the yield curve is.
kid: Count how many sweets your friend gives for a long wait and for a short wait, then take one from the other. The bigger the difference, the more waiting pays.
detail: The term spread measures the slope of the yield curve by subtracting a short-maturity yield from a long-maturity yield on bonds of the same issuer. The most quoted versions are the US 2s10s (10-year minus 2-year Treasury yield) and the 3m10y (10-year minus 3-month), which the New York Fed uses in its recession-probability model. A positive spread means a normal curve; a negative one means inversion. Because the short end tracks the policy rate and the long end reflects growth and inflation expectations, the spread is a compact read on whether policy is tight relative to the outlook. Indian analysts watch the gap between the 10-year G-sec and short-term T-bill yields. Do not confuse the term spread with a credit spread, which compares bonds of the same maturity but different default risk.
example: Say the US 10-year Treasury yields 4.40% and the 2-year yields 3.90%, so the 2s10s spread is +50 basis points. If the 2-year then rises to 4.60% with the 10-year unchanged, the spread becomes −20 basis points and the curve has inverted.
formula: Term spread = Long-term yield − Short-term yield (for example, 10-year yield − 2-year yield)

short: The extra yield investors demand for holding one long-term bond instead of buying short-term bonds again and again over the same period.
kid: If you lend your toy for a whole year, you cannot change your mind halfway. So you ask for a little extra sweet for being stuck with that promise.
detail: The term premium is the part of a long-term yield not explained by expected future short-term rates. If markets expect the policy rate to average 4% over ten years but the 10-year bond yields 4.5%, the roughly 0.5 percentage point gap is the term premium: pay for the risk that rates, inflation or bond supply turn out differently than expected. It cannot be observed directly, so it is estimated with models, such as the New York Fed's ACM model, and estimates differ. It was near or below zero for much of the late 2010s, when central banks bought huge amounts of bonds, and rose again in 2023 as inflation and government borrowing worried investors. A rising term premium can lift mortgage and corporate borrowing costs even when central banks hold rates steady. Do not confuse it with the term spread, which is directly observable.
example: Say investors expect the 1-year rate to be 4% this year and 5% next year. Under pure expectations, a 2-year bond would yield about 4.5% a year; if it actually yields 4.8%, the estimated term premium is about 0.3 percentage point, or 30 basis points.
formula: Term premium ≈ Long-term yield − Average expected short-term rate over the bond's life

short: The idea that long-term interest rates simply reflect the average of the short-term rates investors expect over the same period.
kid: If lending your toy for one day earns 1 sweet today, and you think tomorrow will also earn 1 sweet, lending it for two days should earn 2 sweets. No more, no less.
detail: Expectations theory says the yield on a long-term bond equals the average of the short-term rates investors expect over its life, so buying a 2-year bond should earn the same as buying a 1-year bond and reinvesting for another year. The pure version assumes investors do not care which maturity they hold and demand no extra pay for lending longer. Its key implication is that the slope of the yield curve is a forecast: an upward slope means markets expect short rates to rise, and an inverted curve means they expect cuts. It underlies the reading of implied forward rates from the curve. Its weakness is that long yields usually exceed the short rates that actually follow, so the curve slopes upward more often than rates rise. That gap is the term premium, which liquidity preference theory adds.
example: Say the 1-year rate is 5% and investors expect the 1-year rate a year from now to be 7%. Expectations theory predicts a 2-year yield of about 6% a year; exactly, √(1.05 × 1.07) − 1 ≈ 5.995%.
formula: (1 + 2-year yield)^2 = (1 + 1-year rate today) × (1 + expected 1-year rate next year)

short: The idea that investors prefer short-term bonds, so they must be paid extra to hold long-term ones, which makes yield curves usually slope upward.
kid: You like having your toys close so you can play whenever you want. If someone wants to borrow one for a long time, you ask for a bigger thank-you.
detail: Applied to the yield curve, liquidity preference (or liquidity premium) theory says long-term yields equal the average of expected short-term rates plus a premium that grows with maturity. Investors prefer short, easily sold bonds because long bonds swing more in price when rates change and tie money up for longer, so they need extra pay to hold them. This explains why the curve normally slopes upward even when no one expects rates to rise, fixing the main weakness of pure expectations theory. It also means an upward slope is not, on its own, a forecast of higher rates. The name echoes John Maynard Keynes, whose liquidity preference theory explains the level of interest rates through people's demand to hold cash; that is a related but different idea, so check which one a textbook means.
example: Say the 1-year rate is 5% today and is expected to stay at 5% next year, so pure expectations theory predicts a 2-year yield of 5%. If investors demand a 0.4 percentage point liquidity premium, the 2-year bond yields about 5.4%, and the curve slopes upward despite flat expectations.
formula: Long-term yield = Average expected short-term rate + Liquidity (term) premium

short: The idea that short-term and long-term bonds trade in separate markets with different buyers, so supply and demand in each set its own yield.
kid: Some kids only swap stickers and others only swap marbles. How much a sticker is worth depends on the sticker kids, not the marble kids.
detail: Market segmentation theory says investors and borrowers stick to particular maturities and do not switch, so the yield curve is really a collection of separate markets. Banks and money market funds mainly buy short-dated paper to match their short-term liabilities, while pension funds and life insurers buy long bonds to match payments due decades later. The yield at each maturity is therefore set by supply and demand within that segment, not by expectations about future rates. The theory helps explain why heavy government issuance at one maturity, or central bank buying under quantitative easing, moves yields there. In India, demand from insurers and provident funds for long-dated government securities has helped shape the long end. Its weakness is the strict assumption that investors never cross segments; preferred habitat theory relaxes it.
example: Say the government shifts ₹50,000 crore of a year's planned borrowing from 10-year bonds to 40-year bonds. Market segmentation theory predicts that the extra 40-year supply pushes 40-year yields up and the reduced 10-year supply lets 10-year yields ease, regardless of anyone's forecast for short-term rates.

short: The idea that investors favour certain bond maturities but will switch to others if paid enough extra yield to move.
kid: You love sitting by the window on the bus. You will only move to another seat if someone gives you a sweet for it.
detail: Preferred habitat theory, proposed by Franco Modigliani and Richard Sutch in 1966, blends expectations theory with market segmentation. Each investor has a favoured maturity range, its habitat, set by when it needs its money: a bank near the short end, a pension fund at the long end. Investors leave their habitat only if the extra yield elsewhere pays them for the risk of a mismatch. So yields reflect expected short-term rates plus premiums that depend on supply and demand in each maturity range, and those premiums can be positive or negative. The theory is widely used to explain how central bank bond buying and changes in government issuance alter the shape of the curve. The common mistake is treating it as identical to segmentation: here, markets are linked, just not perfectly.
example: Say a life insurer prefers 30-year bonds yielding 6.8%, while 15-year bonds yield 7.0%. If the insurer needs at least 0.5 percentage point more to accept the mismatch, the 0.2 point gap is not enough, so it stays at 30 years; with the 30-year yield unchanged, it would switch only if 15-year yields rose above 7.3%.

short: The interest rate today for money lent from now until one specific future date, with everything repaid in a single payment at the end.
kid: If you lend your toy today and get all your sweets back in one go on your birthday, the sweets you ask for are for that one wait.
detail: A spot rate, also called a zero rate or zero-coupon yield, is the annual yield on an investment that starts today and pays a single cash flow at one future date, with no coupons in between. Each maturity has its own spot rate, and plotting them gives the spot, or zero, curve. Spot rates are the correct discount rates for valuing bonds and other fixed cash flows: each payment is discounted at the spot rate for its own date, rather than at one yield to maturity for the whole bond. They can be read from zero-coupon instruments such as treasury bills and government STRIPS, or bootstrapped from coupon bond prices. Be careful: in currency markets, 'spot rate' means the exchange rate for immediate delivery, which is a different thing.
example: Say the 1-year spot rate is 6% and the 2-year spot rate is 7%. A bond paying ₹100 in one year and ₹1,100 in two years is worth 100 / 1.06 + 1,100 / 1.07^2 = ₹94.34 + ₹960.78 = ₹1,055.12.
formula: Price of a zero-coupon bond = Face value / (1 + s_t)^t, where s_t is the t-year spot rate

short: An interest rate fixed or implied today for a loan that starts later, such as a one-year loan beginning a year from now.
kid: Today you and your friend agree how many sweets you will get for lending your toy next week. You fix the deal now, even though the lending starts later.
detail: A forward rate is the interest rate for a period that begins in the future, locked in or implied by today's prices. Implied forward rates come from the spot curve: if you can lend for two years at one rate, or for one year and then roll over, the forward rate is the second-year rate that makes both choices equal. Working them out across maturities gives the forward curve. Traders use forward rates to price forward rate agreements, interest rate swaps and futures, and to read what the market is pricing for future policy rates. Under pure expectations theory, forward rates equal expected future spot rates; in practice they also contain a term premium, so they tend to overstate where rates end up. In currency markets, 'forward rate' means a future exchange rate, a different concept.
example: Say the 1-year spot rate is 6% and the 2-year spot rate is 7%. The implied 1-year rate starting in one year is 1.07^2 / 1.06 − 1 = 1.1449 / 1.06 − 1 ≈ 8.01%. Lending for two years at 7%, or for one year at 6% and then one year at 8.01%, gives the same result.
formula: f(1,1) = (1 + s2)^2 / (1 + s1) − 1, where s1 and s2 are the 1-year and 2-year spot rates and f(1,1) is the 1-year rate starting in one year

short: The coupon rate at which a bond of a given maturity would sell for exactly its face value today.
kid: Imagine a toy whose sticker price is exactly what everyone pays, with no discount and nothing extra. The par rate is the size of the thank-you that makes the price match the sticker.
detail: A par rate, or par yield, is the coupon rate that makes a bond's price equal to its face value, or par, when its cash flows are discounted at the current spot rates. Because a bond priced at par has a yield to maturity equal to its coupon, the par rate is also that bond's yield. Plotting par rates across maturities gives the par curve, the form in which many governments and data providers publish benchmark yield curves, since newly issued bonds are usually sold close to par. Swap rates are also par rates: the fixed rate on a new swap is set so the swap is worth zero at the start. The par, spot and forward curves contain the same information in different forms, and mixing them up leads to discounting errors.
example: Say the 1-year spot rate is 6% and the 2-year spot rate is 7%. A 2-year bond with ₹100 face value sells at par if its annual coupon C satisfies C / 1.06 + (100 + C) / 1.07^2 = 100, which gives C ≈ ₹6.97, a par rate of about 6.97%.
formula: Par rate = (1 − d_n) / (d_1 + d_2 + ... + d_n), where d_t = 1 / (1 + s_t)^t is the discount factor for year t (annual coupons)

short: A step-by-step method of working out zero-coupon (spot) rates from the prices of coupon-paying bonds, starting with the shortest maturity.
kid: To climb a ladder, you stand on the first step to reach the second, then on the second to reach the third. You use what you already found to find the next one.
detail: Bootstrapping builds a spot, or zero-coupon, curve from the prices of coupon bonds, par rates or swap rates. You start with the shortest maturity, whose spot rate is known directly. For the next bond, you discount its early coupons at the spot rates already found and solve for the single unknown spot rate that makes the present value equal the bond's price. Repeating this maturity by maturity produces the whole curve, which is then used to price bonds, swaps and other fixed cash flows and to derive forward rates. Real-world curve building adds interpolation and smoothing, because bonds do not mature on every date. Outside fixed income, bootstrapping also means building a self-funded startup on its own revenue without outside investors, and statisticians use the word for a resampling method; here it means the curve technique.
example: A 1-year zero-coupon bond gives a spot rate of 6%. A 2-year bond paying a 7% annual coupon on ₹100 face trades at ₹100. Solve 7 / 1.06 + 107 / (1 + s2)^2 = 100: since 7 / 1.06 = 6.6038, 107 / (1 + s2)^2 = 93.3962, so s2 ≈ 7.04%.
formula: Price = C / (1 + s1) + C / (1 + s2)^2 + ... + (C + F) / (1 + sn)^n, solved for sn using the spot rates s1 to s(n−1) already found

hl: front end of the yield curve
short end of the yield curve
short: The short-maturity part of the yield curve, bonds and bills maturing within about two years, which moves closely with the central bank's policy rate.
kid: Picture a row of piggy banks: some you can open next week, some only when you are grown up. The front end is the ones you can open soon.
detail: The front end, or short end, of the yield curve covers the shortest maturities: overnight money-market rates, treasury bills and government bonds out to about two years, though some desks stretch it to three or five. Front-end yields are driven mainly by the current policy rate and what markets expect the central bank to do at its next few meetings, so they react sharply to inflation data and central bank statements. The US 2-year Treasury yield is the most watched front-end benchmark; in India, the 91-day T-bill and overnight rates such as the weighted average call rate track the RBI's repo rate. Money-market funds, banks managing liquidity and corporate treasurers operate here. Do not confuse front-end yields with policy rates themselves: the front end often moves before the central bank acts, because it prices expectations.
example: Say a central bank's policy rate is 6.50% and the 1-year bill yields 6.70%, implying markets expect hikes. After a weak inflation reading, traders price cuts instead and the 1-year yield falls to 6.25%, a 45 basis point move at the front end while the policy rate has not changed.

hl: long end of the yield curve
short: The part of the yield curve covering bonds that mature in 10 to 30 years or more, shaped by long-run views on growth and inflation.
kid: Some piggy banks you can open soon, and some only when you are all grown up. The long end is the ones you have to wait the longest to open.
detail: The long end, or back end, of the yield curve covers the longest maturities, generally 10-year bonds and beyond, out to 30, 40 or even 50 years. Long-end yields depend less on the next central bank decision and more on expected average rates over decades, long-run inflation, government borrowing and the term premium investors demand. Because long bonds have high duration, small yield changes produce big price swings, so the long end is where bond gains and losses are largest. Pension funds and insurers are natural buyers, since their liabilities stretch decades ahead; in India, they anchor demand for 30- and 40-year government securities. Long-end yields feed into mortgage rates and the discount rates used to value shares. Definitions vary: some traders call the 5- to 10-year sector the 'belly' of the curve and reserve 'long end' for 20 years and beyond.
example: Say a 30-year bond has a modified duration of about 17 and a 2-year bond about 1.9. If both yields rise by 1 percentage point, the 30-year bond loses roughly 17% of its price (a little less once convexity is counted) and the 2-year only about 1.9%, which is why moves at the long end hit portfolios hardest.

short: The yearly return on a 10-year US government bond held to maturity, and one of the most closely watched interest rates in the world.
kid: When a very big country borrows from people for ten years, it promises a small thank-you every year. People all over the world watch the size of that thank-you.
detail: The 10-year Treasury yield is the yield to maturity on the most recently issued 10-year US Treasury note. Because Treasuries are the global benchmark for low-default-risk assets, this yield is a reference rate for the world: US mortgage rates track it closely, many corporate bonds are priced as a spread over it, and analysts use it as the risk-free rate in valuation models. It moves with expectations for Federal Reserve policy, inflation and growth, plus the term premium. When it rises, bond prices fall and highly valued growth stocks tend to suffer; it can also pull money toward the dollar and lead foreign investors to sell emerging-market assets, including Indian bonds and shares. India's own benchmark is the 10-year G-sec yield. Check the live rates board for current levels rather than relying on remembered figures.
example: Say a newly issued 10-year Treasury note with a 4% coupon trades at par, so it yields 4%. If its yield rises to 4.5%, its price falls to about $96.0 per $100 of face value. And if equity investors demand 5 percentage points over this yield, their required return rises from 9% to 9.5%.

short: The yearly return on a 2-year US government bond held to maturity, closely tied to what markets expect the Federal Reserve to do with rates.
kid: When a very big country borrows for just two years, the small thank-you it promises shows what people think will happen very soon.
detail: The 2-year Treasury yield is the yield to maturity on the most recently issued 2-year US Treasury note. Because two years is short, it mostly reflects where investors expect the Federal Reserve's policy rate to average over that period, making it the market's cleanest real-time read on Fed expectations. It reacts sharply to jobs reports, inflation data and Fed speeches, often moving well before the Fed itself does. Set against the 10-year yield, it gives the 2s10s term spread; when the 2-year rises above the 10-year, the curve is inverted, a widely watched recession signal. Indian traders follow it because shifts in expected Fed policy affect the rupee, foreign portfolio flows and the RBI's room to move. Do not confuse it with the federal funds rate, for which the Fed sets a target range; the 2-year is a market price.
example: Say the federal funds rate is 4.25% and the 2-year Treasury yields 3.75%, 50 basis points lower, suggesting markets expect rate cuts. If a strong jobs report lifts the 2-year to 4.00%, traders have priced out about 25 basis points of those expected cuts.
